meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

That house is old.

I have no idea at all.

examples.text: Я человек чистый. Я вообще не вор.
examples.trans: I'm an honest man. I'm not a thief at all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with / from', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Share with everyone.
I'm with Dad.
Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лететь'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'flew off / lost your mind'.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и слететь вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and flew off on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют слететь.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You're greedy!
Have you got any more?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'but, after all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: But you've still got some.
But I know.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common masculine noun meaning 'guests' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.
You have visitors!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'меяться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'are laughing', paired with 'засмеяться'.

examples.trans: Don't laugh!
The children are laughing.
Don't laugh. Read me the number.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'gentlemen' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Gentlemen, I apologise.
This is Mr Petrov.
Gentlemen, I apologise. The money will be there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.en: must, need to, it is necessary
meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: It needs a wash.
We need to do even more.
It needs a wash!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from/out of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The town hall called me.
He's from Moscow.

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, я уже знаю. Мне звонили из мэрии.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, I already know. The town hall called me.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('ancient').

examples.trans: The monastery is our ancient history.
The monastery is our ancient history!

examples.text: Здесь был утрачен древний оригинал летописи.
examples.trans: Here the ancient original of the chronicle was lost.

meanings.note: Relational adjective formed with the Slavic suffix '-ский' ('pertaining to'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('Scottish').

examples.text: Шеф говорит, что это очень шотландский выбор.
examples.trans: The chef says that this is a very Scottish choice.

examples.text: У нас сегодня просто шотландский день в ресторане.
examples.trans: We are having a simply Scottish day at the restaurant today.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'clan / lineage' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть род.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always clan.
The chef immediately noticed where the clan was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, near, with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ой, кажется, у вас сломан нос!
examples.trans: Oh, it looks like your nose is broken!

examples.text: Завтра у меня важное собеседование на работу.
examples.trans: Tomorrow I have an important job interview.

examples.text: Значит, у нас с тобой много общего.
examples.trans: So you and I have a lot in common.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'us', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'нятый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('customary').

examples.text: Шеф говорит, что это очень принятый выбор.
examples.trans: The chef says that this is a very customary choice.

examples.text: У нас сегодня просто принятый день в ресторане.
examples.trans: We are having a simply customary day at the restaurant today.

meanings.en: to walk, to go on foot
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go (regularly)'.

examples.trans: The boy walks on crutches.
I walk to work.

examples.text: Мальчик ходит на костылях. А она ещё и активистка.
examples.trans: The boy walks on crutches. And she's an activist, too.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'in skirts / kilts' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть юбка.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'рядок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'order' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order.
Everything is in complete order.

examples.text: Теперь давай всё по порядку. Скажи мне, сколько ты им должна?
examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order. Tell me, how much do you owe them?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'them', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: They are building a centre.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'said', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: What did you say?
Excuse me, where's the metro?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'зорить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'disgraces'.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'themselves', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

meanings.note: Agent/instrument noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-тель' ('-er'). Common masculine noun meaning 'hotel' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть отель.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always hotel.
The chef immediately noticed where the hotel was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (polite/plural)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: As you all know...

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.en: course of medical treatment or study
meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'course, regimen' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: We prescribed a course of antibiotics.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'our', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'трана'). Common feminine noun meaning 'country' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The whole country is laughing at you!
It is a big country.

examples.text: Над тобой вся страна смеётся! Все видели, как ты из окна летел.
examples.trans: The whole country is laughing at you! Everyone saw you fly out the window.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'претить').

examples.trans: But Anikeev forbade it!

examples.text: Аникеев же запретил! Нам нельзя пить.
examples.trans: But Anikeev forbade it! We mustn't drink.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'паганда'). Common feminine noun meaning 'propaganda' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть пропаганда.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always propaganda.
The chef immediately noticed where the propaganda was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'традиционный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('non-traditional').

examples.text: Шеф говорит, что это очень нетрадиционный выбор.
examples.trans: The chef says that this is a very non-traditional choice.

examples.text: У нас сегодня просто нетрадиционный день в ресторане.
examples.trans: We are having a simply non-traditional day at the restaurant today.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'of room service' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть рум-сервис.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always of room service.
The chef immediately noticed where the of room service was.

meanings.note: Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common feminine noun meaning 'little lady' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть дамочка.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always little lady.
The chef immediately noticed where the little lady was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here.
There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'does', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: What are you doing?
I'm making dinner.
Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's always like that.
There's always a way out.
She's offended. She's always like that.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: I can't today.
That can't be.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.en: to tie the score, recoup, equalize, bounce back
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'ыграться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to win back / get even', paired with 'отыгрываться'.

examples.trans: The football players managed to tie it up in the end.

examples.text: Там сейчас счёт три-три, наши отыгрались!
examples.trans: The score there is three-three now, our guys tied it up!

examples.text: Они двадцать лет подряд так не отыгрывались.
examples.trans: They had not tied it up like that for twenty years in a row.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: I'm in the office now.
I'll be right there.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'ис-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'полнять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'I am fulfilling', paired with 'исполнить'.

examples.trans: They're singing La Marseillaise.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и исполнять вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and I am fulfilling on time.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('other, different').

examples.trans: Could we go somewhere else?
That's a different building.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'wish' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть желание.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always wish.
The chef immediately noticed where the wish was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is your coffee.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.
Your boss is here.
